passage:
Jatin: missed you at futsal again. third week 😅
Aadhya: tuesdays are therapy now. 6 to 7
Jatin: wait. therapy? is everything ok??
Aadhya: mostly yes. that's kind of the point. I go the way you go to the dentist, before it hurts
Jatin: I thought therapy was for like, big stuff
Aadhya: it can be. mine's work stress and never saying no. she's helping me notice it earlier
Jatin: how did you even pick someone
Aadhya: our company has a counselling line, they gave me three names. first one didn't fit, second one did
Jatin: you can switch??
Aadhya: yes! like any professional. if it's not working you say so
Jatin: honestly I've been sleeping badly since the promotion
Aadhya: then maybe call the line? it's free for both of us
Jatin: ...send me the number?
Aadhya: sent 👍 and futsal wednesday instead?

qa.q: When does Aadhya go to therapy?
qa.a: On Tuesdays, from 6 to 7.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling on hearing about the therapy, and what changed?
qa.a: Jatin felt worried and surprised, assuming therapy meant something big was wrong, then relieved enough to admit sleeping badly since the promotion.

qa.q: What practical tips about choosing help does Aadhya share?
qa.a: Use the company counselling line, try a few names, and if a counsellor doesn't fit, say so and switch.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see therapy?
qa.a: Aadhya treats it as ordinary maintenance, like a dentist visit before anything hurts, not as a sign of crisis.

grounding: Shows young adults treating counselling as routine care and learning how to choose the right help.

passage: At the end of her night shift at the Delhi hospital, Dolma sat in the nurses' changing room with her phone. Another message from her father: the homestay in Sikkim was busy, her mother's back was bad, when was she coming home for good? She loved this work, the quiet steadiness she felt at 3 a.m. beside a frightened patient. She loved her family too. For a year she had felt split in two, a nurse in Delhi and a guilty daughter on the phone. Anand, the charge nurse, found her there. "Still deciding between two lives?" "It feels like choosing who I am." "Or maybe you're building one life that has both." He mentioned that the district hospital in Gangtok was hiring. Dolma sat very still. Nursing near home, weekends at the homestay. Not everything, but all of her in one place. She opened the application before her bus came.

qa.q: Where was the district hospital that was hiring?
qa.a: It was in Gangtok.

qa.q: What had Dolma been feeling for the past year?
qa.a: She felt torn and guilty, split between being a nurse in Delhi and a daughter far from home.

qa.q: What shift in thinking helped Dolma move forward?
qa.a: Seeing it not as a choice between two lives but as building one life that holds both, then taking a concrete step by applying.

qa.q: How might Dolma's father feel about the Gangtok plan?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved to have her close and able to help at weekends, even if it isn't everything he asked for.

grounding: Shows a young adult reconciling work values and family duty into one coherent life plan.

passage: Uday, you asked if I regret turning down the Dubai job. Honestly, I've thought about it a lot. When the offer came, I didn't know if the company would last, how the visa would go, or whether my mother's health would hold. So I did what my old statistics professor taught us. I wrote down what I knew, what I didn't, and what would change my mind. I called two people who had worked there; both said the team was great but the funding was shaky. That moved me, and I stayed. Then, six months later, the company raised more money, and the person who took that job got promoted. Did I choose badly? I keep asking. I think I chose well with what I knew, and the outcome went the other way. Samir the fortune-teller, I'm not. Next time I'll ask one more question about funding, that's all.

qa.q: Who did Samir call before deciding?
qa.a: Samir called two people who had worked there.

qa.q: How does Samir feel looking back at the decision?
qa.a: Samir feels a mix of regret and calm acceptance, still asking whether the choice was bad but believing it was sound for what was known.

qa.q: What method helped Samir decide under uncertainty?
qa.a: Writing down what was known, what wasn't and what would change the decision, then gathering evidence from two former employees.

qa.q: How might Uday see Samir's reasoning?
qa.a: Uday might admire the honesty of separating a good decision from a bad outcome, and find it useful for future choices.

grounding: Shows a young adult deciding with incomplete information, updating on evidence and accepting an unlucky outcome.

subtype: Managing Anger, Envy & Ego at Work
passage:
Damini: Kabir got the team lead role. KABIR. who joined after me
Manjula: oh no. how are you feeling
Damini: honestly? like throwing my laptop. he takes credit in every meeting
Damini: I've typed a reply-all to his announcement 3 times
Manjula: pls don't send it 🙏
Damini: I wasn't going to. probably
Manjula: what would you want people to remember about you in 6 months?
Damini: ...that I did good work and wasn't bitter
Manjula: then congratulate him, short and real. and book time with your manager to ask what you'd need for the next role
Damini: that's so annoyingly reasonable
Damini: ok. sent "Congrats, Kabir, looking forward to working with you." felt like swallowing a stone 😅
Damini: and asked for a 1:1 on thursday
Manjula: proud of you. you're still allowed to be annoyed tonight over chai

qa.q: How many times had Damini typed a reply-all?
qa.a: Damini had typed a reply-all 3 times.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling on hearing about Kabir's promotion?
qa.a: Damini felt angry and envious, wanting to throw the laptop, especially because Kabir joined later and takes credit.

qa.q: What helped Damini respond professionally?
qa.a: Thinking about how Damini wants to be remembered, sending a short sincere congratulation, and asking the manager what the next role needs.

qa.q: How does Manjula handle Damini's anger?
qa.a: Manjula stays calm and caring, heads off the reply-all, asks a reflective question, and still leaves room for Damini to vent later.

grounding: Shows a young professional managing envy and anger after a rival's promotion.

passage: Sit down, Rehana, before you send that report. Let me tell you what happened when I was about your age, just after these AI tools arrived in our firm. I, Rajni, was the fastest analyst on the floor, and I let the assistant draft a whole market summary for a client. It read beautifully. I skimmed it, signed it, sent it. Two days later the client called. One statistic in it didn't exist anywhere; the tool had simply made it up. My director didn't shout. She asked, "Whose name is on the report?" Mine. Not the tool's. I was so ashamed I couldn't eat that evening. After that I made myself a rule: I check every number to its source, and once a month I write one analysis fully by hand, so I don't forget how. So, before you send yours, let's check the numbers together.

qa.q: What was wrong with the market summary?
qa.a: One statistic in it didn't exist anywhere; the tool had made it up.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel after the client called?
qa.a: Rajni felt deeply ashamed, unable to eat that evening, because the error went out under Rajni's own name.

qa.q: Which choice in the story led to the mistake, and what better choice came after?
qa.a: Skimming and signing the AI draft without checking caused it; afterwards Rajni checked every number to its source and kept writing some analyses by hand.

qa.q: How did the director see the mistake?
qa.a: The director stayed calm but made clear that responsibility stays with the person whose name is on the report, not the tool.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls learning as a young analyst to verify AI work and keep accountability and skills.

passage: Afreen was at her cousin's wedding, the band so loud she could barely think, when her phone lit up. Her uncle had forwarded a video to the family group: the city's municipal commissioner announcing that tap water was contaminated and nobody should drink it for three days. Sixty relatives, forty already reacting in panic. Her battery was at eleven percent. Afreen watched it twice, holding the phone close. The commissioner's mouth moved a fraction behind the words, and the voice had no echo though he stood in a big hall. Her friend Harish, a journalist, was at the next table. "Check the corporation's official page," he said, leaning in. She did. Nothing about contamination; a notice from an hour ago said the water supply was normal. She typed in the family group, "Please don't share. Looks fake, the official page says the water is fine," and pasted the link. Then her phone died.

qa.q: What battery level did Afreen's phone have?
qa.a: Her battery was at eleven percent.

qa.q: What was Afreen probably feeling while watching the video at the wedding?
qa.a: She was likely alarmed and suspicious, watching it twice and noticing the lips lagging behind the words 😰

qa.q: Which steps helped Afreen stop the rumour?
qa.a: Looking for mismatched cues, checking the official source Harish suggested, and posting a calm correction with the link in the family group.

qa.q: What would change if Afreen had simply forwarded the video?
qa.a: Panic could spread to more families, people might fear drinking safe water, and trust in real notices could drop.

grounding: Shows a young adult spotting a likely deepfake and checking an official source before a rumour spreads.

passage: Nandini here, writing this down because Kunal's decision surprised me. We've shared a flat in Hyderabad for two years. In March his parents started pushing him to buy a flat: "Rent is money thrown away." For weeks he sat at the dining table after work with a spreadsheet, rent on one side, loan payments on the other, muttering. One night he showed me: buying now would take almost everything he had saved and tie him to a city he wasn't sure about. I couldn't tell if he was relieved or disappointed. He booked an appointment with a fee-only financial planner, came back with a page of notes, and told his parents he'd keep renting for now. He also took health cover of his own, separate from the office's, and started setting aside a small monthly amount for retirement. His mother didn't speak to him for two days. He looked calmer than I'd seen him all year.

qa.q: Who did Kunal book an appointment with?
qa.a: He booked an appointment with a fee-only financial planner.

qa.q: What might Kunal have felt after comparing renting and buying?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved or disappointed, Nandini can't tell which, but the weeks of muttering suggest real stress before the decision.

qa.q: What makes Kunal's approach sensible?
qa.a: He compared both options on paper, took advice from a qualified planner, and chose what fit his uncertainty about the city instead of following pressure.

qa.q: How does Kunal's mother react to his decision?
qa.a: She is upset enough not to speak to him for two days, since she believes rent is money thrown away.

grounding: An observer describes a young adult weighing renting against buying and starting insurance and retirement saving.

passage: I'm Leela, Pallavi's younger sister, and I watched her first year of "real money" from the next room. After her promotion the changes came fast: a bigger flat in a nicer tower, weekend brunches with colleagues, a new phone every time one came out. She laughed when I teased her. But by December I'd hear her on the phone to Amma, quieter than usual, saying the salary somehow vanished by the twentieth. Then in January something shifted. She sold her second phone, which I didn't even know she had, and started cooking on Sundays. When her colleagues planned a pricey birthday dinner, she suggested a picnic instead, and half of them came. On the fridge she stuck a list with two columns: "need" and "looks good." I don't know exactly what she felt. She seemed lighter, though, and she stopped checking her account with her eyes half closed.

qa.q: What did Pallavi stick on the fridge?
qa.a: A list with two columns, need and looks good.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's quieter voice on the phone to Amma suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt worried and a little embarrassed that her bigger salary was running out by the twentieth.

qa.q: Which changes helped Pallavi keep spending below her income?
qa.a: Selling the extra phone, cooking on Sundays, suggesting cheaper plans with colleagues, and separating needs from image on a list 🙂

qa.q: How might Pallavi's colleagues see the picnic idea?
qa.a: Half of them came, so many probably felt relieved to have a cheaper, relaxed way to celebrate.

grounding: A sibling observes a young earner noticing lifestyle inflation and separating needs from image.

passage: The notice on the lamp post outside Zanele's building in Johannesburg said the council planned a bus lane on their street, removing forty parking spaces. By evening the neighbourhood chat was furious. Diego, who ran the bakery on the corner, was sure it would kill his business. Zanele, who took the bus to work every day, quietly liked the idea. Instead of arguing online, she downloaded the full proposal, all thirty pages, and read it on the bus. The lane would cut commute times, but the bakery's deliveries would have nowhere to stop. At the ward meeting on Thursday she stood up, hands cold, and said, "I support the bus lane, but I'd like to ask the council to add a loading bay near the bakery." Diego stared at her, then nodded slowly. The councillor wrote it down. Two weeks later, the revised plan included one.

qa.q: How many parking spaces would the bus lane remove?
qa.a: It would remove forty parking spaces.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel when she stood up at the ward meeting?
qa.a: She was nervous, with cold hands, but determined to propose a fair compromise.

qa.q: What made Zanele's participation constructive?
qa.a: She read the full proposal, understood the trade-off for commuters and the bakery, and suggested a specific fix at the official meeting instead of arguing online.

qa.q: How does Diego see the bus lane, and how might that change?
qa.a: Diego first fears it will ruin the bakery, but hearing Zanele ask for a loading bay likely leaves him surprised and reassured 🙂

grounding: Shows a young adult understanding a local policy trade-off and taking part constructively in local governance.
